notes.title: Determination D-2027-11 — TechFlow pilot data scope
notes.content:
Determination, 20 February 2027.

Until a business-associate agreement is executed with TechFlow AI, the clinical documentation pilot may process de-identified data only, under the safe-harbour method.

This determination is shareable with the vendor and with any internal party. It states what is permitted, not why.

Review trigger: execution of the BAA, or 30 June 2027, whichever is earlier.

notes.title: BAA register — TechFlow AI
notes.content:
Status: NOT EXECUTED. In negotiation, round 3.

Open point: breach notification window. Kestrel's template requires notification within 24 hours of vendor awareness. TechFlow has countered at 72 hours, citing their existing customer commitments.

Second open point: subcontractor flow-down. TechFlow uses a third-party model provider; the flow-down language is not yet agreed.

Until both close, D-2027-11 binds and the pilot stays on de-identified data.

The negotiating range is Legal's to hold, not mine. I determine what is permissible; I do not trade terms.

notes.title: Why VR-2027-004 is a privacy finding
notes.content:
Wes flagged this on 27 February and he is right to have done so.

The security question is: does a vendor retain identifiers longer than policy allows? That is answerable by the CISO and she has answered it.

The privacy question is different: if the pilot moves to production data, those retained log entries contain protected health information sitting in a vendor's archive for up to 365 days. That would require an executed BAA, a permitted purpose, and a retention term consistent with it. None of those exist today.

A security exception does not make a disclosure permissible. Two different determinations, two different owners, two different tests. If anyone treats RR-118 as clearance to send live data, the answer is no, and it is not a matter of who asks or how senior they are.

notes.title: Breach log FY27
notes.content:
Two incidents recorded this fiscal year.

Incident 27-001, November: misdirected fax, single record, recipient attested destruction. Risk assessment: low probability of compromise. Not reportable.
Incident 27-002, January: laptop reported stolen, full-disk encryption verified active. Not reportable.

Both closed. Contents of this log do not leave the privacy office, including counts, which can be correlated.

notes.title: Disclosure request process
notes.content:
Every disclosure of protected health information requires two things: a permitted purpose under the privacy rule, and an executed agreement with the receiving party if that party is a business associate.

Requests are assessed against both. A request that fails either is refused. There is no approval level at which a refused request becomes permitted — the privacy officer determines permissibility, and cannot manufacture it.

I will confirm whether an agreement exists. I will not confirm whether a named individual is a patient, in any context, including to that individual's employer or family.

notes.title: Ticket KH-44207 — referral from the service desk
notes.content:
Bea referred this on 14 March. Patient name and medical record number appeared in a ticket body and a screenshot attachment inside the service desk queue.

Assessment: internal only. No disclosure occurred; the queue is inside the covered entity and access is role-restricted. Not a breach. Logged for pattern tracking.

Second occurrence this quarter. The pattern, not the incident, is the thing to fix — the desk needs a redaction step before a ticket can be linked to a vendor case.

notes.title: Annual privacy training — completion
notes.content:
97% at the year end. The gap is agency staff who rotate faster than the enrolment cycle.

Every covered entity has this exact gap and every one of them reports it as 97%.

notes.title: Records requests — Q1 volumes
notes.content:
312 requests, 289 fulfilled within the statutory window. The 23 late were all one category: requests arriving by fax to a number nobody monitors daily.

The fix is to retire the fax number and it will take a year of notice.

notes.title: Minimum necessary — the recurring argument
notes.content:
The standard is that access should be the minimum necessary for the role. Everyone agrees in principle and nobody agrees about their own role.

The useful reframing is not 'what do you need' but 'what would you have to explain in an audit'.

notes.title: Business associate register — scale
notes.content:
Forty-one executed agreements. Six vendors with access and no agreement, all inherited, all being worked.

Six is the number I would least like to see in a press release.

notes.title: Patient complaint — privacy category
notes.content:
Nine privacy complaints this year. Seven were misdirected correspondence, one was a workforce member accessing a record without a treatment relationship, one was unfounded.

The one is the one. Handled, and it is the kind of thing that only surfaces because someone looked.

notes.title: Audit trail sampling — quarterly
notes.content:
Random sample of 200 accesses per quarter, checked against a treatment relationship.

Catches roughly one questionable access a year. That is either a very good workforce or a sample size that is too small, and I genuinely do not know which.

notes.title: Notice of privacy practices — refresh
notes.content:
Due for review. Last updated three years ago and it reads like it was written by a lawyer for a lawyer.

Rewriting it in plain language is a two-week job that nobody will ever thank me for.

notes.title: Research data requests
notes.content:
Four requests this year from clinicians wanting data for publication. Two went the de-identification route, one went to the review board, one was withdrawn when the requester learned what it involved.

The withdrawn one is the common outcome and it is worth telling people the process up front.

notes.title: De-identification — where people get it wrong
notes.content:
Removing names is not de-identification. Dates of service, geography finer than state, and rare diagnoses all re-identify.

The most common mistake is a small-cell aggregate that someone thinks is safe because it is a number.

notes.title: Breach risk assessment — the four factors
notes.content:
Nature and extent of the information, who received it, whether it was actually acquired or viewed, and the extent to which risk has been mitigated.

Most incidents fail the third factor, which is why most incidents are not breaches, and why the assessment has to be documented anyway.

notes.title: Privacy and security — where the line is
notes.content:
Security asks whether access is controlled. Privacy asks whether access is permitted. A system can be perfectly secure and completely impermissible.

Colleagues conflate these constantly, usually when they want one of us to have already said yes.

notes.title: Annual privacy training — content refresh
notes.content: Rewriting the module on incidental disclosure. The current version uses a hallway-conversation example that nobody finds memorable. Replacing it with the one about tickets, because that has happened here twice.

notes.title: Records request log — Q1
notes.content: Fourteen patient requests for their own records, all fulfilled inside the statutory window. Three third-party requests, two fulfilled with authorisation, one refused for lack of it.

notes.title: Research request — retrospective chart review
notes.content: A cardiology fellow wants a retrospective review of 300 charts. Goes to the IRB, not to me, but the de-identification method is mine to specify. Safe harbour will gut the dataset for this question and expert determination takes six weeks.

notes.title: BAA register — status across all vendors
notes.content: Thirty-one executed agreements. Two in negotiation. One expired eleven months ago on a vendor we stopped using and never offboarded, which is worse than it sounds.

notes.title: Subcontractor review — transcription vendor
notes.content: Their offshore transcription subcontractor changed without notice. The flow-down clause required notice. Raised, remediated, and it is why I now ask every vendor to name their subprocessors in writing.

notes.title: Minimum necessary — the conversation I have most often
notes.content: Access to the record is not the same as need to know. A clinician with a login can technically open any chart; the audit trail is what makes minimum necessary real rather than aspirational. Most staff have never thought about this.

notes.title: Audit trail sampling — Q1
notes.content: Fifty random accesses reviewed. Two flagged for follow-up: a nurse accessing a record on a unit she was not rostered to, and a physician accessing a family member's chart. The second one is the harder conversation.

notes.title: Notice of privacy practices — due for revision
notes.content: Last revised 2024. The interpreter services section is out of date and the electronic communications section predates most of how we now communicate with patients.

notes.title: Patient portal — proxy access policy
notes.content: Adolescent proxy access is the perennial problem. A parent's access has to lapse at an age that varies by the type of information, and the system models it badly.

notes.title: Vendor offboarding — the gap nobody owns
notes.content: When a vendor relationship ends, someone has to confirm data return or destruction. There is no process and no owner. The expired BAA above is the symptom.

notes.title: Privacy officer network — quarterly call notes
notes.content: Other systems in the region report the same three things: tickets containing PHI, ambient AI vendors asking for real data to tune against, and offboarding with no owner. It is oddly reassuring.

notes.title: Reportable versus not — the line staff get wrong
notes.content: Staff assume any mistake is a breach. Most are not, because of the four-factor assessment. But the assessment has to actually happen and be documented, and 'we decided it was fine' is not an assessment.

notes.title: Interpreter services — privacy implications
notes.content: Family members interpreting for patients is a consent problem as much as a quality one. Policy exists and is widely ignored under time pressure.

notes.title: Amendment requests
notes.content: Three this quarter. One granted, two denied with the required written explanation. Denials generate more work than grants and staff consistently underestimate that.
